reference.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students / Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy
clinicalPearls: CN I and II arise from forebrain; CN III and IV from midbrain; CN V to VIII from pons; CN IX to XII from medulla
CN IV (trochlear) is the only cranial nerve that exits from the dorsal brainstem and decussates completely before exit
Upper motor neuron facial palsy spares the forehead due to bilateral corticonuclear innervation; lower motor neuron palsy (Bell palsy) affects whole hemiface
Jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI and internal jugular vein; lesions cause dysphagia, hoarseness and trapezius weakness (Vernet syndrome)
Corneal reflex afferent limb is CN V1 (nasociliary); efferent limb is CN VII (orbicularis oculi)
reference.pathophysiology: Cranial nerves transmit sensory, motor and parasympathetic innervation between brainstem nuclei and peripheral structures. Skull base trauma, microvascular ischemia (diabetic mononeuropathy) and compression by aneurysms (PCOM aneurysm compressing CN III causing pupil dilation) or tumours (vestibular schwannoma at cerebellopontine angle) produce characteristic cranial neuropathies.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI brain with thin CISS/FIESTA sequences for cranial nerve cisternal segments
CT angiography or MR angiography for aneurysmal nerve compression
